messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Tran was a 54-year-old divorced electrician who had spent most of her adult life moving between job sites, carrying tool belts up stairwells and across hospital campuses, never imagining that the building where she had once gone for a routine appointment would become the place her body learned to fear. Three years earlier, she had developed a life-threatening infection that sent her to the emergency department in a rush of monitors, antiseptic air, and urgent voices. She remembered the heaviness of her own breathing as the staff moved around her bed, the sharp hospital smell, and the date stamped in her mind because it had happened near the same week every year since. Even now, the anniversary of that admission would arrive and unsettle her before she had consciously thought about it. What frightened Marisol most was not just that she had nearly died, but that her body had seemed to betray her without warning; since then, she had felt as if any change in breathing could mean danger.

In the months after the illness, those cues began to hit her hard in ordinary places. A coworker pausing to catch his breath on a hot job would make her go still. The smell of disinfectant in a clinic hallway, or the faint antiseptic odor in a hardware store that serviced a medical building, could make her chest tighten and her stomach drop. On the anniversary week, her body would become constantly tense and ready to react, as if she had to brace for the same crisis again. She described her body reacting before her mind had time to think: her heart would race, her shoulders would lock, and she would feel strong physical reactions before she could tell herself she was safe. Those moments pushed her into her habits of coping. She tried to pretend it had happened to someone else, as though the memory belonged to a different woman entirely, and she spent long stretches imagining how life would have been different if the infection had never occurred—whether she would still be married, whether she would still feel like herself, whether she would have kept her old confidence on the job. When the thoughts came, they dulled the moment for a while, but they also left her more unsettled and more aware of how easily her body could turn against her. The more she felt that tension and alarm in her body, the more she leaned on those mental strategies to get through the day.

At work, the pattern had become self-reinforcing. Marisol started avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations, arranging her life so she would not have to pass the emergency entrance when she was doing electrical repairs for a building contractor. She would ask coworkers to take any job near a clinic or medical office, and she delayed routine checkups even when her family urged her to go. Yet the avoidance did not free her from reminders; it made them feel more potent. Because she was so determined not to enter a hospital or sit through an examination, even the prospect of an appointment could set off the same alertness days in advance. If she saw an ambulance outside a store, or heard heavy breathing in a crowded break room, she would be flooded with a bodily jolt that seemed to confirm what she feared. In those moments she would slip back into pretending it had happened to someone else, or she would mentally rehearse the life she might have had if the illness had not stolen that year from her. But the more she withdrew into those thoughts, the more her body stayed on edge, tense and watchful, ready for danger before she had finished making sense of what she had heard or smelled.

By the time she came to treatment, Marisol was exhausted by the way the anniversary, heavy breathing, and hospital smells kept reactivating the same surge of bodily alarm, and by how quickly her strategies turned into another trap. She had begun missing opportunities at work because she would not take assignments near medical facilities, and her reluctance to seek even a routine examination had started to worry her adult daughter. Marisol said she finally wanted help because she was tired of living as though any breath could be a warning. What she feared most was that her body would keep reacting first and that she would spend the rest of her life pretending the illness belonged to someone else, while secretly waiting for it to happen again.
